title: Bonnie and Clyde
summary: Josh and Chuck profile Bonnie and Clyde, the Depression-era outlaw couple who led the Barrow Gang across the Southern and Midwestern US in 1932–1934. They cover Clyde Barrow's childhood poverty, his prison time at the Eastham prison farm, and Bonnie Parker's background and poetry. The episode follows the gang's robberies and the cop killings, the Joplin, Missouri shootout, the Iowa park gunfight, and the Eastham prison break. It then covers the 1934 Louisiana ambush by Frank Hamer's Texas Rangers, the funerals and souvenir hunting, the dragnet against family and associates, the disputed Joplin-era murder attributed to Bonnie and the likely real killer Henry Methvin, and the 1967 film's legacy and the death car's later display. The episode closes with a listener mail about Eleanor Roosevelt and Pulp Fiction.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about a song, a listener named Anthony, and the American Experience documentary, then frame the episode as true crime and folk hero.

segments.title: Clyde Barrow's childhood and early prison time
segments.summary: Clyde's Depression-era poverty in Texas, his first arrest at seventeen for car theft, and Bonnie's background and early marriage. Clyde's Eastham prison farm sentence, his assault and killing of an inmate, and another inmate taking the blame.

segments.title: Clyde's release and joining the gang
segments.summary: Clyde cuts off toes to avoid labor, is paroled after his mother petitions, and resumes robbery. Bonnie joins with Ralph Foltz. The hosts discuss the couple's romance and their appeal.

segments.title: Early murders and the gang's growth
segments.summary: Timeline of early 1932 to early 1933: Foltz's arrest, the April 1932 store murder of John Butcher, the August 1932 killing of deputy Eugene Moore, the Christmas killing of Doyle Johnson, recruitment of W.D. Jones, and the January 1933 ambush killing of Malcolm Davis.

segments.title: Famous photos of the gang
segments.summary: W.D. Jones took the famous photos of the gang in early 1933, including the colorized image of Clyde lifting Bonnie. Bonnie's small size is mentioned.

segments.title: Joplin, Missouri shootout
segments.summary: Buck and Blanche join the gang. The gang stays thirteen days in Joplin before neighbors call police. A gunfight kills two officers, Harry McGinnis and Wes Harryman. W.D. is wounded and the gang drives to Shamrock, Texas.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Press coverage and Bonnie's poem
segments.summary: Newspapers found the gang's Joplin hideout and undeveloped photos, making them famous. Bonnie's poem 'The Story of Suicide Sal' is discussed, along with an AI-generated song based on it. Bonnie's personality is discussed.

segments.title: Folk hero status and Clyde's letter to Henry Ford
segments.summary: Clyde's letter to Henry Ford praising Ford V8 cars. Folk hero status tied to Depression bank foreclosures. True crime magazines exaggerated their bank robberies. The gang's cautious communication with family.

segments.title: Car crash and burns
segments.summary: A bad car crash leaves Bonnie with third-degree burns on her leg, from fire or battery acid, and she limps for life. Hot-wiring and early car batteries are noted.

segments.title: Missouri and Iowa gunfights
segments.summary: Gunfights in Missouri and Iowa, including a fight where Buck and Blanche were wounded and then arrested. W.D. Jones leaves the gang and returns to Texas, where he is sentenced to six years.

segments.title: Eastham prison break and new members
segments.summary: Clyde helps break Raymond Hamilton, Joe Palmer, Hilton Biby, and Henry Methvin out of Eastham, killing two guards. Buck dies after capture. More cop killings follow in Grapevine and Oklahoma.

segments.title: Hamilton's split from the gang
segments.summary: Raymond Hamilton is recaptured, is sentenced to death, and escapes death row before being recaptured. The gang had split from him after a falling out.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break.

segments.title: Frank Hamer and the Methvin deal
segments.summary: Texas Rangers under Frank Hamer and the Bureau of Investigation pursue the gang. Hamer comes out of retirement. Henderson Jordan, a Louisiana sheriff, is approached by the Methvin family, who offer to trade Bonnie and Clyde for leniency for their son Henry.

segments.title: Grapevine-area ambush, May 1934
segments.summary: In May 1934 lawmen ambushed Bonnie and Clyde on Highway 154 near the Methvin family's car, with a wheel removed as bait. Officers fired automatic rifles. Bonnie was shot about 26 times and Clyde about 17.

segments.title: Funerals, souvenir hunting, and posthumous poems
segments.summary: Bodies taken to Dallas. Souvenir seekers tried to take body parts and car pieces. Separate funerals drew crowds. Emma Parker kept them apart. Posthumous poems and the failed effort to rebury them together are described.

segments.title: Dragnet and the Joplin-era disputed murder
segments.summary: Family and friends were rounded up in a dragnet, with sentences of up to a few years. A disputed killing of a patrolman is attributed to Bonnie, but historians believe Henry Methvin was the killer and was covered up.

segments.title: Aftermath of Henry Methvin, Blanche, and the death car
segments.summary: Methvin was paroled in 1942 and died six years later, possibly hit by a train. Blanche served six years, wrote a memoir, and worked in Dallas. The death car and guns were fought over by families and later toured carnivals and went to Buffalo Bill's in Primm, Nevada.

segments.title: 1967 film and legacy
segments.summary: The 1967 film directed by Arthur Penn, starring Faye Dunaway and Warren Beatty, revived interest and set up later violent films. The hosts mention the death car and shirt at Buffalo Bill's.

segments.title: Wrap-up
segments.summary: Hosts end the Bonnie and Clyde discussion and move to listener mail.

segments.title: Listener mail from Sam and Lisa
segments.summary: Listener Sam writes about a Josh fact that his wife doubted, about Eleanor Roosevelt's treatment that became Pulp Fiction. He mentions being a long-time listener.
